---
title: "4. Community structure (PCoA)"
format:
  html:
    toc: false
---

*Analyse community composition using Bray–Curtis distances and visualise patterns with a Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).*

### Normalise counts to relative abundances

First, convert ASV counts to relative abundances per sample. Normalising in sparse space avoids creating a large dense intermediate matrix:

```r
col_totals <- Matrix::colSums(merged$counts)
norm_sparse <- Matrix::t(Matrix::t(merged$counts) / col_totals)
norm_counts <- as.matrix(norm_sparse)
```

`norm_sparse` retains the sparse structure and is reused in [6](tutorial-06-randomforest.qmd). `norm_counts` is the dense version required by `vegdist`.

### Calculate Bray–Curtis distances

Compute pairwise [Bray–Curtis distances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bray%E2%80%93Curtis_dissimilarity){target="_blank"} (beta-diversity):

```r
bray_dist <- as.matrix(vegdist(t(norm_counts), method = "bray"))
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Scaling to larger datasets.** The dense matrix `norm_counts` (ASVs × samples) and the n×n distance matrix can become large. Two recommended steps before this point when working with many ASVs or samples:

1. **Filter rare ASVs** to reduce `norm_counts` before the `as.matrix()` call — e.g. keep only ASVs present in ≥5% of samples:
   ```r
   keep_asvs <- which(Matrix::rowSums(norm_sparse > 0) / ncol(norm_sparse) >= 0.05)
   norm_counts <- as.matrix(norm_sparse[keep_asvs, ])
   ```
2. **Subsample samples** if n > ~1 000: `pcoa()` performs a full eigendecomposition (O(n³)), which becomes slow above a few thousand samples.
:::

### Run PCoA

Perform [Principal Coordinates Analysis](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/principal-coordinates-analysis-pcoa-a-comprehensive-guide/){target="_blank"} on the distance matrix:

```r
pcoa_res <- pcoa(bray_dist, correction = "cailliez")
```

### Plot PCoA results

We plot samples in PCoA space using the first two axes. Point colour shows habitat type; point shape shows sampling method. Two panels separate the two datasets for clarity.

```r
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE))
par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), xpd = TRUE, cex.axis = 1)

xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[1] * 100), "%)")
ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[2] * 100), "%)")

# Panel: Malaise trap
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     pch = pch, col = "white", bg = "white",
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Malaise trap")
points(pcoa_res$vectors[DS_malaise, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[DS_malaise, 2],
       pch = pch[DS_malaise], col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat[DS_malaise],
       cex = 1.4)

# Panel: Soil/litter
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     pch = pch, col = "white", bg = "white",
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Soil/litter")
points(pcoa_res$vectors[DS_soillitter, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[DS_soillitter, 2],
       pch = pch[DS_soillitter], col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat[DS_soillitter],
       cex = 1.4)

# Legend
plot.new()
legend("center", bty = "n",
       legend = names(habitat_cols),
       pt.bg  = habitat_cols,
       pch    = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.1,
       title  = "Habitat")
```

Interpretation: the PCoA shows whether community composition is structured by habitat type, sampling method, or both.
